8B

Key ideas

Newton’s laws of motion

Definitions

Force diagram: a diagram that shows the relative magnitude and direction of all of the forces acting on a body. The forces are shown acting from the centre of mass of the object.
Normal force: the force that a surface applies to a body resting on it. The force is always applied perpendicular to the surface and prevents the body falling through the surface.
Gravitational field strength: a theoretical region of space around a mass where the gravitational force can be experienced by other masses. The gravitational field strength is expressed in N kg−1^{-1}−1, which is equivalent to the acceleration due to gravity in m s−2^{-2}−2.
System: a collection of objects that interact with each other

Formulas

Fnet=maF_{\text{net}} = maFnet​=ma

8B

New knowledgeNewton’s first law

Newton’s laws of motion

Newton’s first law states that an object in a state of rest or travelling at a constant velocity will remain in its state of motion unless acted upon by a net force.

If a car is at rest or travelling at a constant velocity, then the net force on the car is zero.

Consider the vertical forces when the car is at rest.

The normal force acting on the car provided by the ground balances the gravitational force acting on the car by Earth.

Figure 8B–2 The forces on a car at rest and a car moving at a constant velocity are balanced. This means that the car at rest will remain at rest and the car moving at a constant velocity will continue to move at a constant velocity.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 225
8B

New knowledgeNewton’s first law

Newton’s laws of motion

For a car that is moving on a straight road at a constant velocity, the horizontal forces of air resistance and rolling friction are balanced by the driving force on the car by the road, and the normal force balances the force gravitational force acting on the car by Earth.

It is contrary to our usual daily experience that an object will continue with a constant velocity indefinitely as long as the sum of the forces acting on the object are zero.

This is because in our experience objects will come to rest as a result of friction, because friction causes a net force on objects that directly opposes their state of motion.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 226
8B

New knowledgeNewton’s second law

Newton’s laws of motion

Newton’s second law states that the acceleration experienced by a body is directly proportional to the net force on the body and inversely proportional to the mass of the body.

This law is often expressed in terms of the following formula. [Formula 8B–1] When determining the net force on a body, it is often helpful to draw a force diagram.

The force vectors can be added to find the net force vector.

For example, calculate the acceleration of a 1150 kg car that has a driving force of 4000 N forwards and a drag force of 2000 N.

Figure 8B–3 Force diagram of an accelerating car (left) and vector diagram of the same accelerating car (right)
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 227
8B

New knowledgeNewton’s second law

Newton’s laws of motion

The force diagram to the left and the vector diagram to the right in Figure 8B–3 show that the net force on the car will be 2000 N forwards (also by Newton’s second law, the force due to gravity and normal force vectors will cancel as there is no acceleration in the vertical, leaving 4000 N – 2000 N = 2000 N).

The acceleration can then be determined: a=Fnetm=20001150=1.74 m s−2a = \frac{F_{\text{net}}}{m} = \frac{2000}{1150} = 1.74\text{ m s}^{-2}a=mFnet​​=11502000​=1.74 m s−2 forwards

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 228
8B

New knowledgeSame acceleration, different forces

Newton’s laws of motion

It is important to remember that while two or more bodies are moving with the same acceleration, the force on each of the bodies will not be the same unless the masses are the same.

For example, if three balls of mass 1 kg, 2 kg and 3 kg are all dropped from the same height, they will all accelerate towards the surface of Earth at the same rate, 9.8 m s−2^{-2}−2 (if air resistance is ignored).

However, to have the same acceleration, the forces on the balls must all be different.

Another fundamental idea is that the only way to cause a body to accelerate is by applying a net force on the body.

Figure 8B–4 Comparison of the forces on three balls of mass 1 kg, 2 kg and 3 kg, all accelerating due to gravity
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 239
8B

New knowledgeSame acceleration, different forces

Newton’s laws of motion

The body will then accelerate in the same direction as the direction of the net force.

This means that the direction of the acceleration and the direction of the velocity are independent.

For example, if a car is approaching a red light and the car brakes, the car’s velocity will be forwards but the acceleration and therefore the net force on the car will be backwards.

Similarly, if a projectile is fired vertically upwards, as soon as the thrust force during the firing is gone, the ball will be accelerating down, since the only force acting on the projectile is the force due to gravity (if air resistance is ignored).

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 2310
8B

New knowledgeSame acceleration, different forces

Newton’s laws of motion

The projectile may be moving up, but its upwards velocity is constantly decreasing until the projectile is momentarily stationary at the maximum height, after which point the ball’s velocity will be downwards and increasing.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 2311
8B

New knowledgeNewton’s third law

Newton’s laws of motion

Newton’s third law states that every action force has an equal and opposite reaction force.

Newton’s third law describes the force interaction between two separate bodies.

For example, if two bodies, A and B, come into contact with each other, then the force on A by B will be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force on B by A. Fon A by B=−Fon B by AF_{\text{on A by B}} = -F_{\text{on B by A}}Fon A by B​=−Fon B by A​ This equation describes the fact that the force pairs are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction.

Notice that the size of the object does not matter; as shown in Figure 8B–5, even though object A is very large and object B is very small, the forces on both objects have the same magnitude.

Figure 8B–5 The action and reaction pair when two bodies come into contact. Vector lines show that the forces are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 2412
8B

New knowledgeNewton’s third law

Newton’s laws of motion

Forces are always in pairs, including gravitational, magnetic and electrostatic forces.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 2413
8B

New knowledgeNormal force

Newton’s laws of motion

Imagine a heavy box, labelled A, that is in free-fall close to Earth’s surface.

When the box is in free-fall, the force of gravity acts to accelerate the box to the ground.

The downward gravitational force on box A by Earth is paired with the upwards gravitational force of box A pulling on Earth.

Imagine that box A is now placed on a table B.

Figure 8B–9 Earth acts to pull A towards it and A acts to pull Earth up towards it.
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 2614
8B

New knowledgeNormal force

Newton’s laws of motion

Box A no longer falls (accelerates down), which means that the net force on the box is zero.

Therefore, as the box rests on the table, the force due to gravity acting on the box must be balanced by an upwards force provided by the table’s surface.

This upwards force is known as the normal force and is often expressed as NNN or FNF_\text{N}FN​.

If you were to push down on box A, it would still not move, which means that the net force on the box is still zero.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 2615
8B

New knowledgeNormal force

Newton’s laws of motion

This means that the normal force has increased to balance the force due to gravity on the box as well as the additional force of you pushing down on the box.

Equally, if you apply a force on the box that is opposite to the force due to gravity, the normal force will reduce in size.

It is important to note that the force due to gravity on box A and the normal force are not force pairs even though they are quite often equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 2616
8B

New knowledgeForce due to gravity

Newton’s laws of motion

As you read this, you are probably sitting in a chair.

The gravitational attraction to Earth is pulling you down.

Take a moment to think what the pair for this force is.

Many people will incorrectly say that the force pair is the normal force of the chair acting on themselves.

Figure 8B–11 The action–reaction pairs of a person being pulled down, in contact with Earth’s surface (left) and falling (right)
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 2717
8B

New knowledgeForce due to gravity

Newton’s laws of motion

This cannot be correct as Newton’s third law describes an interaction between two bodies; when you sit down, the interaction is occurring between your body and Earth.

The force of gravity is a non-contact force.

That means that if you were in free-fall, gravity would still act to pull you down.

Since you have your own mass, things can be gravitationally attracted to you.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 2718
8B

New knowledgeForce due to gravity

Newton’s laws of motion

Therefore, the force pair is Earth being gravitationally attracted to your mass.

The force due to gravity can be expressed mathematically as: [Formula 8B–2] The gravitational force acts from the centre of mass of all objects.

Remember that mass refers to the body’s resistance to acceleration when a force is applied and this does not change.

However, the gravitational force (sometimes referred to as the weight force) is a force and would change if you were on the Moon, for example, since it has a different gravitational field strength.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 2719
8B

New knowledgeApplying Newton’s laws

Newton’s laws of motion

Newton’s laws can be applied to solve a variety of problems. [Worked examples 8B–1 to 8B–3]

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 2820
8B

New knowledgeChanging normal forces

Newton’s laws of motion

Imagine that you are standing in an lift that is moving up and down.

You have an accurate scale that measures the force that you exert on the surface of the lift and therefore the force that the surface exerts on you (the normal force).

You wonder, how would the force change with the motion of the lift?

When you stand on the scale there are only two forces acting on you, the force due to gravity, mgmgmg, and the normal force, NNN.

Figure 8B–13 The forces acting on a person in a lift
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 3221
8B

New knowledgeChanging normal forces

Newton’s laws of motion

We can sum the forces in the vertical as shown: ∑Fvertical=N−mg\sum F_{\text{vertical}} = N - mg∑Fvertical​=N−mg The force due to gravity, mgmgmg, is negative as it acts down.

Since a force is just the product of mass and acceleration, the equation can be expressed as: mavertical=N−mgma_{\text{vertical}} = N - mgmavertical​=N−mg The acceleration, averticala_{\text{vertical}}avertical​, is the vertical acceleration of the lift.

This can then be rearranged to make the normal force, NNN, the subject: [Formula 8B–3] The scale is reading the normal force, not the force due to gravity.

The normal force and the force due to gravity will only be equal when the lift is either stationary or moving at a constant velocity.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 3222
8B

New knowledgeChanging normal forces

Newton’s laws of motion

When the lift is accelerating up, the normal force will be greater than the force due to gravity, and when the lift is accelerating down, the normal force will be less than the force due to gravity.

You may ask yourself what would the normal force be if the lift cable snapped and the lift accelerated down with an acceleration of 9.8 m s−2^{-2}−2.

The answer might surprise you: the normal force would be zero; you would be falling down with an acceleration of 9.8 m s−2^{-2}−2 but not getting any normal reaction force from the floor of the lift.

This is what happens when astronauts and cosmonauts orbit Earth in space stations.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 3223
8B

New knowledgeInclined planes

Newton’s laws of motion

On a slope, such as the one shown in Figure 8B–15, an object will have three forces acting on it: the force due to gravity, which acts vertically down; the normal force, NNN, which acts perpendicular to the surface; and the friction force, fff, which acts parallel to the slope.

When an object is stationary on an inclined plane, all of the forces will balance.

This means that the normal force, which is the force by the surface on the object, will be equal in magnitude but opposite in direction to the component of the force due to gravity that acts perpendicular to the surface.

It also means that the friction force, applied by the surface on the object, is equal in magnitude but opposite in direction to the component of the force due to gravity that acts parallel to the slope.

Figure 8B–15 The forces acting on an object that is stationary on an inclined plane
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 3324
8B

New knowledgeInclined planes

Newton’s laws of motion

This means that when an object is stationary on an inclined slope the equations on Figure 8B–15 are true. [N=mgcos⁡θN = mg\cos\thetaN=mgcosθ, f=mgsin⁡θf = mg\sin\thetaf=mgsinθ] If the object is on a frictionless surface, then it will be accelerated down with a force of mgsin⁡θmg\sin\thetamgsinθ.

Since F=maF = maF=ma, the acceleration of the slope can be determined to be: F=mgsin⁡θF = mg\sin\thetaF=mgsinθ, ma=mgsin⁡θma = mg\sin\thetama=mgsinθ Therefore: [Formula 8B–4]

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 3325
8B

New knowledgeApplication of motion: the physics of car safety

Newton’s laws of motion

In 2019, 1195 people were killed on Australian roads compared to 3798 in 1970, even though there are now many more cars on the roads.

Over the past 40 years, an understanding of the physics of car crashes has led to three major innovations in car safety.

These three major innovations are seatbelts, air bags and crumple zones.

In any collision involving a car, there is a rapid change in momentum that occurs.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 3526
8B

New knowledgeApplication of motion: the physics of car safety

Newton’s laws of motion

This rapid change in momentum can create large forces on the occupants, which can cause injury or death.

Before 1972, seatbelts were not required to be worn in Australia.

If a passenger is not wearing a seatbelt during a collision, then according to Newton’s first law of motion, the passenger will continue in their state of motion.

This means if someone crashes at 90 km h−1^{-1}−1, the car will begin to slow but the occupant will continue to move at 90 km h−1^{-1}−1 until they hit something like the windscreen, steering wheel or dashboard.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 3527
8B

New knowledgeApplication of motion: the physics of car safety

Newton’s laws of motion

This will apply an unbalanced force on them, causing them to slow down.

The introduction of the seatbelt meant that in a car crash, an unbalanced force would be applied across the person’s shoulders and hips, the strongest parts of their body, so the person would slow down with the car.

However, a person’s head would often continue to move forwards and hit the steering wheel, resulting in injury or death.

It wasn’t until 1980 that the air bag helped to solve this problem.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 3528
8B

New knowledgeApplication of motion: the physics of car safety

Newton’s laws of motion

During a crash, the air bag will inflate very rapidly.

When the occupant’s head hits the air bag, the force spreads out more evenly and the collision lasts longer.

The impulse will be the same for the crash and as I=FavΔtI = F_{\text{av}}\Delta tI=Fav​Δt, by extending the time of the collision the average force on the occupant is reduced.

Early cars were made to be strong and rigid, as it was believed that this would protect the occupants.

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 3529
8B

New knowledgeApplication of motion: the physics of car safety

Newton’s laws of motion

But modern cars have crumple zones.

These zones in the front, rear and sometimes even sides of the car are designed to crumple in a collision.

Similar to an air bag, the crumple zones increase the time of the collision, thereby reducing the average force on the occupants.

Modern cars still have a rigid compartment that holds the occupants as you wouldn’t want that part to crumple, otherwise it would crush the occupants. [continues p. 451: electric vehicles, active safety (Figures 8B–16 to 8B–18, photos)]

Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 3530

8B

We doForce on touching blocks

Newton’s laws of motion
A 45 N force to the right is used to push two blocks, A and B, on a frictionless surface. Block A has a mass of 2 kg and block B has a mass of 1 kg. When they are pushed, both blocks move as one. a Calculate the acceleration of the two blocks. b What is the force on block B by block A? c What is the force on block A by block B?
Key idea · Formula 8B–1 Newton’s second lawFnet=maF_{\text{net}} = maFnet​=ma

Working

a As the two blocks move as one, you need to add the masses together.
a=Fnetm=452+1=15 m s−2a = \frac{F_{\text{net}}}{m} = \frac{45}{2+1} = 15\text{ m s}^{-2}a=mFnet​​=2+145​=15 m s−2
Therefore, the acceleration of the blocks is 15 m s−2^{-2}−2 to the right.
b As B is accelerating at 15 m s−2^{-2}−2, you need to find the force that will accelerate it at this rate.
Fon B by A=ma=(1)(15)=15 NF_{\text{on B by A}} = ma = (1)(15) = 15\text{ N}Fon B by A​=ma=(1)(15)=15 N
Therefore, the force on block B is 15 N to the right.
c Every action has an equal and opposite reaction. The action force is the force that block A applies on block B so the reaction force will be the force that block B applies to block A. Therefore, the force on block A is 15 N to the left.
a 15 m s−2^{-2}−2 right; b 15 N right; c 15 N left
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 28, Worked example 8B-138
8B

We doForce in a pulley system

Newton’s laws of motion
A mass of 9 kg, initially at rest, lies on a frictionless table. It is attached to a mass of 3 kg, which hangs freely off the table by a string and frictionless pulley system. Assume the string's mass is negligible. a What is the acceleration of the system of the two joined masses? b Calculate the tension in the string.
Key idea · Formula 8B–1 Newton’s second lawFnet=maF_{\text{net}} = maFnet​=ma

Working

a The first step is to determine the net force acting on the system. Since the mass of 3 kg is hanging freely, gravity will provide a net downwards force. As the mass of 3 kg falls, the pulley system will transfer some of the force, via the string, to the block of 9 kg, causing it to slide to the right.
Therefore: Fnet=mg=(3)(9.8)=29.4 NF_{\text{net}} = mg = (3)(9.8) = 29.4\text{ N}Fnet​=mg=(3)(9.8)=29.4 N
Newton’s second law can now be applied to calculate the acceleration of the system (note that the two masses are added as the whole system is being accelerated):
a=Fnetm=29.49+3=2.45 m s−2a = \frac{F_{\text{net}}}{m} = \frac{29.4}{9+3} = 2.45\text{ m s}^{-2}a=mFnet​​=9+329.4​=2.45 m s−2
b The tension in the string is a result of the string pulling on the mass of 9 kg and accelerating it at 2.45 m s−2^{-2}−2. Therefore, the tension can be found by applying Newton’s second law:
Fnet=ma=(9)(2.45)=22.05 NF_{\text{net}} = ma = (9)(2.45) = 22.05\text{ N}Fnet​=ma=(9)(2.45)=22.05 N
a 2.45 m s−2^{-2}−2; b 22.05 N
Cambridge VCE Physics Units 1&2, Chapter 8, p. 29, Worked example 8B-239
8B

We doTension in a train system

Newton’s laws of motion
A steam engine with a mass of 20 000 kg is towing two carriages, each with a mass of 10 000 kg. The engine is connected to both of the carriages by cable X and the two carriages are connected by cable Y. As the engine leaves the station, it produces a driving force of 35 000 N. You may assume there is no rolling or air friction in this system. A diagram of this situation is shown below. a Calculate the acceleration of the engine and carriage system. b Calculate the tension in cable X. c Calculate the tension in cable Y.
Key idea · Formula 8B–1 Newton’s second lawFnet=maF_{\text{net}} = maFnet​=ma

Working

a Since the engine is towing both of the carriages, they are all part of the same system and will all accelerate at the same rate. This means that the masses can be added together to find the magnitude of the acceleration:
a=Fnetm=35 00010 000+10 000+20 000=0.875 m s−2a = \frac{F_{\text{net}}}{m} = \frac{35\,000}{10\,000 + 10\,000 + 20\,000} = 0.875\text{ m s}^{-2}a=mFnet​​=10000+10000+2000035000​=0.875 m s−2
b Cable X is towing two carriages. This means it is subject to the tension required to accelerate both carriages at 0.875 m s−2^{-2}−2:
F=ma=(10 000+10 000)(0.875)=1.75×104 NF = ma = (10\,000 + 10\,000)(0.875) = 1.75\times10^{4}\text{ N}F=ma=(10000+10000)(0.875)=1.75×104 N
c Cable Y is towing one carriage. This means it is subject to the tension required to accelerate one carriage at 0.875 m s−2^{-2}−2:
F=ma=(10 000)(0.875)=8.75×103 NF = ma = (10\,000)(0.875) = 8.75\times10^{3}\text{ N}F=ma=(10000)(0.875)=8.75×103 N
a 0.875 m s−2^{-2}−2; b 1.75×1041.75\times10^{4}1.75×104 N; c 8.75×1038.75\times10^{3}8.75×103 N

Newton’s laws of motion
A 96 kg man stands on a set of scales which measures the force that he applies to the floor inside an elevator. What is the force that the scales read when the elevator is: a at rest b moving at a constant velocity of 1.5 m s−1^{-1}−1 down c moving with an upward acceleration of 0.2 m s−2^{-2}−2 d moving with a downward acceleration of 0.35 m s−2^{-2}−2.
Key idea · Formula 8B–1 Newton’s second lawFnet=maF_{\text{net}} = maFnet​=ma

Working

a At rest, the vertical acceleration is zero; therefore: N=m(avertical+g)=(96)(0+9.8)=941 NN = m(a_{\text{vertical}} + g) = (96)(0 + 9.8) = 941\text{ N}N=m(avertical​+g)=(96)(0+9.8)=941 N
b When moving with a constant velocity, the vertical acceleration is zero; therefore: N=m(avertical+g)=(96)(0+9.8)=941 NN = m(a_{\text{vertical}} + g) = (96)(0 + 9.8) = 941\text{ N}N=m(avertical​+g)=(96)(0+9.8)=941 N
c Since the acceleration is up, it will be positive: N=m(avertical+g)=(96)(0.2+9.8)=960 NN = m(a_{\text{vertical}} + g) = (96)(0.2 + 9.8) = 960\text{ N}N=m(avertical​+g)=(96)(0.2+9.8)=960 N
d Since the acceleration is down, it will be negative: N=m(avertical+g)=(96)(−0.35+9.8)=907 NN = m(a_{\text{vertical}} + g) = (96)(-0.35 + 9.8) = 907\text{ N}N=m(avertical​+g)=(96)(−0.35+9.8)=907 N
a 941 N; b 941 N; c 960 N; d 907 N

8B

We doAcceleration on a frictionless slope

Newton’s laws of motion
A 1080 kg car is parked at the top of a driveway on Mt Buller. The driveway is inclined at 19°. a Calculate the magnitude of the normal force on the car by the surface. b Calculate the magnitude of the frictional force by the surface on the car. c On a particularly cold morning the driveway becomes covered in ice and all friction between the surface and the tyres is lost. Calculate the magnitude of the car’s acceleration down the slope.
Key idea · Formula 8B–1 Newton’s second lawFnet=maF_{\text{net}} = maFnet​=ma

Working

You trySection 8B questions Q6

Newton’s laws of motion
A learner driver notices that they have to put their foot on the accelerator pedal in order to maintain a constant velocity. This confuses the driver, who is also a physics student, as they know that acceleration means a change in velocity. How would you explain the observation made by this student? Your answer needs to refer to a specific law of motion.

Working

The accelerator pedal gives fuel to the engine, which allows the car to generate a forward thrust force. Because the car is encountering friction with the road and air resistance, it must have a forward thrust force that is equal in magnitude but opposite in direction so the forces will balance. This is because, according to Newton’s first law, an object will remain at a constant velocity unless acted upon by an unbalance force.

Newton’s laws of motion
Check-in set 1 · Q1 · 8B
If you were to drive down a freeway at a constant speed and then suddenly brake hard, your body would move forward until it is stopped by the seatbelt. Explain this observation using the relevant laws of motion.
When you brake, the car begins to decelerate, however you continue to move forward at the same speed, as the net force on you is zero. When you come into contact with the seatbelt, it applies a force on you that is opposite to your direction of motion, thereby decelerating you.
Check-in set 1 · Q2 · 8B
One of the most famous golf swings was literally out of this world. In 1971, NASA astronaut Alan Shepard took two shots of golf while on the Moon during the Apollo 14 landing. It was noticed that the golf balls flew consistently higher and further than they would on Earth. Use the relevant laws of motion to describe this observation.
According to Newton’s second law of motion, the ball’s acceleration is directly proportional to the force applied to it. On the Moon there is less gravity and air resistance, which means there is less force pulling the ball down and directly opposing its motion. This reduced force means that there is less deceleration on the ball, so it will travel higher and further as it takes a longer time to slow down.
Check-in set 1 · Q3 · 8B
When a set of traffic lights turns green, a car and bike accelerate at the same rate and therefore stay in line for the first 200 m of their journey. Jiang on the bike thinks that the driving force of the bike and the car must be the same, but Alice in the car thinks that the driving force of the bike and the car must be different. Who is correct? Justify your answer.
Alice is correct. Because the car has much more mass than the bike, more force would be required to maintain the same acceleration, given the formula a=Fma = \frac{F}{m}a=mF​.

If the action force of an elephant standing on solid ground is the force due to gravity, which is 39 000 N down, identify and explain the reaction force. Your answer should refer to a specific law of motion. (2 marks)
The force due to gravity is due to the gravitational attraction between Earth and the elephant. According to Newton’s third law, the reaction force will be Earth being gravitationally attracted to the centre of mass of the elephant with a force of 39 000 N.

Apply motion concepts to discuss vehicle safety
Two bumper cars collide head on. Bumper car 27 has a total mass of 310 kg and is travelling at 4.92 m s−1^{-1}−1 east. Car 27 collides with car 13 that has a total mass of 275 kg and is travelling at a velocity of 3.98 m s−1^{-1}−1 west. After the collision car 27 has a velocity of 0.10 m s−1^{-1}−1 east. a Calculate the velocity of car 13 after the collision. Include a direction in your answer. (2 marks) b What is the change in momentum of car 13? Include a direction for your answer. (3 marks) c What is the average force on car 13 during the collision given that the collision lasted for 1.25 seconds? (3 marks) d The occupant of the bumper car complains and says that the force during the collision was too high. Explain one way in which the force on the occupant could be reduced without changing the speed or mass of the car. (2 marks) e Is this an elastic collision? You must use at least two calculations to justify your answer. (3 marks) The occupant of the bumper car complains and says that the force during the collision was too high. Explain one way in which the force on the occupant could be reduced without changing the speed or mass of the car. (2 marks)
The bumper itself could be made to be softer. By making the bumper softer, the time of the collision would increase, and because Favg=IΔtF_{\text{avg}} = \frac{I}{\Delta t}Favg​=ΔtI​, the impulse for a given collision is constant. By increasing the time of the collision the average force would be reduced.
